They love the land on which they live, but they are not so parochial as to love only their own land. They love their land; they love their parish; they love their institutions; they love their province, and they love their country. Once a friend of mine from the Pacific coast asked me what the French-Canadians would do if there were an attack on Vancouver, and what they would do if conscription were applied. The answer came very quickly from a good French-Canadian habitant, who said, " If one part of our country is attacked we shall be ready to go there, so there will be no need of conscription."
That is the understanding of the farmer. He has made sacrifices to acquire his land or to retain the ancestral property. He is at home on his land and is friendly to all those who come to see him. He is willing to help them. There is nothing so nice as the spirit of cooperation that exists in the French-Canadian parishes, and when I visited some parts of Ontario and New Brunswick I was pleasantly surprised to find the same spirit prevailing among the country people of Scotch, Irish and English descent. They are the same; they have the same needs and the same understanding. You may translate into English what is published in the French newspapers and submit it to English-speaking farmers; you may translate into French what is published in the English press and submit it to French-speaking farmers, and you will have the same comments from both. They have the same way of understanding things, and any divergences of opinion are only as to details. They condemn two things, and the first is blind imperialism. They do not agree to that and for a very good reason. They are sentimental with their neighbours and friends, but when it comes to business they reason things out and are sagacious. In the first place, as I have said, they are against blind imperialism ; in the second place they are against extreme nationalism. They are just good Canadians; they love their country and want it to be prosperous. That is their understanding.
They have another quality which is almost a virtue. It is pride in Canada. They are proud of their country; they are happy to live in it, and for them Canada is the first country of the world. That sentiment is very good; the young children in our schools should be taught to love Canada more than any other country, and to be prepared to make sacrifices for Canada. The French-Canadians make sacrifices in the first place for those round them, for their families; then for those in their parish who are not so fortunate; and afterwards they are ready to

help those of the province who are suffering. But if someone should attack Canada they are ready to defend it, because they love this country. But they do not have the same love for the people of central Africa that they have for their fellow citizens of Canada. That is an entirely different matter. If a man like Sir Henry Page-Croft has a coffee plantation in Tanganyika, or some similar place, which he may lose, it makes no difference at all to them. They will not sacrifice anything for the welfare of Sir Henry Page-Croft or any other member of the federation, league or anything like that. They may be interested from a humanitarian point of view that people who live in central Africa or South America should not suffer, but they would otherwise be indifferent to what happens in central Africa, Fiji or other distant parts of the world. They love this country. They have nothing against England; they love their fellow citizens of English, Irish and Scotch ancestry, and they are ready to defend our soil against any aggressors. They are friendly with all.
They do not desire to break empire ties, as has been said, but they want Canada to be considered a self-governing dominion, as has been said many times. It would be much better for us to have an opportunity to decide what we are going to do in external affairs.
I am referring of course to commitments. That would be much better than to be tied to the policy of Great Britain or that of any other country. They decide for themselves; why should we not decide for ourselves as to any assistance we may give to them in due course?
In my humble view, if an emergency occurred, it would be so serious a matter that it would be a hardship to be tied to all the commitments made at Westminster. We should have an opportunity of weighing the pros and cons and of deciding what, if anything, is to be done. Under those circumstances the assistance given by Canada or any other dominion would be prized all the more by Great Britain.
That, sir, is my humble view. If we are indeed a self-governing nation within the empire, then let us act as such. Let us decide what is best for us. I believe it would be much better for Great Britain to follow the example of Canada than for Canada to follow the example of Great Britain. The old countries have much to learn from the new-and this statement is made in the best possible spirit. At times they are subject to prejudice. As I said earlier, an important distinction must be drawn between the British people and the British government. In all those matters I rely on the present government, particularly

maintopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
As I read the new section

maintopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS

maintopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: Would the minister explain the conditions under which cases may be re-opened, and, where the applicant or appellant has evidence of new and substantial character that should be considered by the appeal board, what exactly are the conditions under which that may be brought before the appeal board?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: I take it the conditions are exactly as they stand to-day. There is no change in the act as far as that is concerned.

maintopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
It says that a case can be opened up only by leave of the appeal board of the commission. Subsection 4 states:
An application based upon any error in such decision or in any decision of the court, by reason of evidence not having been presented or otherwise, may be entertained by the commission with the leave of an appeal board of the commission . . . and such appeal board shall have jurisdiction to grant leave in any case in which it appears proper to grant it.
Will that mean a special appeal board? What has the minister in mind in regard to regulations governing such appeals?

maintopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: I understand these powers are the same as are at present vested in the appeal court. The appeal board will have jurisdiction to grant leave in any case in which it appears proper for them to grant it, by reason of new evidence not having been presented, or otherwise. Any application which would have been entertained by the appeal court can be entertained by an appeal board. I do not think there is any difference; it is not intended that there should be.

maintopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: Do I understand the minister to say that by subsection 4 a man who lost an appeal to the appeal court can have a rehearing only by consent of the appeal board?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: Right.

maintopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: Is it now the intention that instead of going to the appeal court for leave to appeal again, it is to the commission? Does that give all those people who have applied for leave to re-open their case before the appeal court, a chance to come again before this appeal board of the commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: On the same terms as they could have submitted their case to the appeal court.

maintopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: I take the last sentence literally.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: It does not mean that every case turned down by the appeal court can now be re-opened, but it does mean that the applicant shall have exactly the same right as he previously had to ask for a re-opening of his case on the presentation of new evidence.

maintopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
He must get consent.

Pension Act Amendment

maintopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: That is what I was going to ask. It is pretty difficult for applicants to secure new evidence. It must be remembered that when they appeared before the quorum, represented by an advocate, they had their cases just as well prepared as it was possible to do. We had the quorum, represented by two members of the pension commission, which passed favourably upon this case. They had the applicant before them. Not only did they have the advocate presenting the applicant's case; they had the applicant in person. They saw his condition, and certainly in many instances the personal appearance of an applicant would suggest sympathetic action. After the quorum had decided favourably on that application, it came back to Ottawa and was appealed by the crown. Then a decision was rendered by a court of appeal two or three thousand miles away, who knew nothing as to the condition of the applicant beyond what was contained in his record or what was presented by the advocate, in fact not as much as was presented by the soldier's representative. When one considers that sixty-two per cent of appeals by the crown were allowed, while practically only two per cent of appeals by applicants were granted, it will be seen that the applicant is placed in a pretty unfortunate position. The question is whether the men on these appeal boards will be the same men who heard the application, as was mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver South.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: They will not.

maintopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
Will there be any change in the members of the board of pension commissioners? There will be three of them this time instead of two; and if by chance one of these cases came before the appeal board on which were two members of the old quorum, together with one new member, hearing the application, they would be placed in rather an embarrassing position; they could not do other than confirm their previous opinion.
I think the minister might reconsider his decision not to permit these cases to come before the appeal board again without new evidence. They have been passed upon once, when all the evidence was presented. The contention may be made that it will cost a great deal of money. Well, it will cost a great deal of money in the future if these men reach a stage where they may be able to present new evidence. The fact remains, it seems to me, that we are hardly doing justice to those men whose cases have been heard and favourably reported upon by a quorum, but who lost out on appeals being taken by 71492-1641
the crown. After all, it is intended that we should do justice to all applicants for pensions. The quorum was created for that purpose; the quorum had these applicants appear in person, and it does not seem unreasonable to ask the minister to permit those applicants to appear once more with such evidence as they presented at the initial hearing.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: There is really no change in this section, which is the old section 70 as brought forward in section 19 of this bill. I think we shall be able to see to it before the bill gets through committee that there will be no doubt whatever that the members of the board who sit in appeal will not be the same people who gave the decision in the first instance. 1 think we can satisfy my hon. friend about that.

maintopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: Does it not stand to reason that the two members of that commission who formed that quorum were just as likely to be right as three members might be now? It is the same question that is being considered-the man's application for pension because of a disability which he claims he has suffered. He was represented by his advocate, and the quorum rendered a favourable decision. My contention is that a quorum before which a man appears in person is better able to decide upon the merit of that application than are three or four members of a court of appeal who have never seen the man, and who would have nothing more to go on than the evidence which was presented by the advocate.

maintopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: As I understand the hon. member for Kootenay West, he is suggesting that an opportunity should be given to rehear successful appeals by the crown. Is that the intention under this bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: That is not at all contemplated by this legislation. I would rather withdraw the bill entirely than do that.

maintopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: With regard to subsection 4 of this section, is it the intention that there will be an appeal board sitting at Ottawa dealing exclusively with applications to reopen.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
I hardly think that would be necessary. This had not struck me before, but just looking at some'figures I have here I am rather astonished to find that of the applications to the pension commission to entertain fresh applications-that is, to the appeal court which is being abolished-there were 572 allowed and 968 disallowed, so that really the pension appeal court, comparatively speaking, if I may put it in that way, was
Pension Act Amendment

generous in granting leave to appeal, perhaps much more so than a great many of us thought until we had the figures before us.

maintopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: Is that in connection with granting rehearings?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: No, that was leave to go before the commission again with a fresh application, apparently based on new evidence. As my hon. friend knows, there were quite a number remitted for rehearing during the period while the appeal court functioned. These were cases in which leave was granted to reopen the applications, apparently on the production of fresh evidence. Of these 572 cases were allowed and 968 disallowed, which is a fairly good batting average.

maintopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: Will the permission to rehear be given only at Ottawa, or is it the intention that boards sitting across the country will have power to grant that request?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: It is wide open; I do not see that there would be any restriction. There is no provision that they shall be heard only at Ottawa; that will be a matter of procedure for the commission itself to deal with. Personally I see no reason why permission should not be granted upon personal application by the applicant in his own district.

maintopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: Then would it not be wiser to cut out the words "such appeal board to be designated by the chairman of the commission from time to time for this purpose?'' The effect would be to give any appeal board the right to order remission.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: That provision is inserted in order that the same people who originally heard the case will not sit on the appeal board.

maintopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
As I read the bill, the only opportunity for rehearing is when the appellant is able to establish an error in the previous decision. Would it not be possible for the minister to consider providing an opportunity for rehearing where the appellant is able to produce new evdence of a substantial nature? I have under my hand at the moment a meritorious case, as is evidenced by the fact that the commission has granted the man a pension under section 24. This man had meritorious service overseas, with a history of nephritis. He was wounded, but at the time of the hearing he was unable to establish the fact that he suffered from trench feet. Since his discharge he has suffered amputation of the right leg, as a result of Buerger's disease. During the evidence a prominent specialist stated that if the history of trench feet could be established it would be related definitely

to the progress of what is known as Buerger's disease and thereby his entitlement to pension would be established. Subsequently this man produced an affidavit from those who served with him and from officers and non-commissioner officers in the battalion stating that at Passchendaele he was definitely treated for trench feet, taken out of the line, given treatment on account of that condition, and so on That is the evidence of a substantial nature which would aid him in establishing entitlement, in view of the medical specialist's opinion given in the case. I suggest cases of outstanding merit, such as the one to which I have referred, where new evidence of a substantial kind is produced, are cases where men should be given leave to enter appeal.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
The subsection reads:
An application based-
One.
-upon any error in such decision or-
Two.
-in any decision of the court, by reason of evidence not having been presented or otherwise, may be entertained by the commission with the leave of an appeal board of the commission.

maintopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: I should like the minister to consider subsection 4 again, if he is to allow appeal boards outside Ottawa to grant rehearings. Apparently there will be quite a few applications, and it seems to me that great confusion will arise unless each appeal board has power to grant a rehearing, rather than having every application first referred back to Ottawa, then having a particular appeal board-say, in Vancouver-designated by the chairman of the commission as an appeal board to hear the particular application.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
My hon. friend had almost convinced me the first time he spoke, but now I am beginning to change my mind. I can see all kinds of practical difficulties in the way if we are to declare in the statute that the appeal board sitting in a district would at all times have the right to re-open a case, because it would be almost physically impossible to have men in the districts who had not already had something to do with that case. We would continually have to be sending men back and forth from Ottawa to Vancouver. I am beginning to think that perhaps the draftsman did not intend to fix the hearing in the district.

Pension Act Amendment

maintopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: That is why I asked the minister at the beginning whether the subsection meant that he was going to set up only one appeal board here at Ottawa to grant leave for rehearing.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: It was not our intention, but I am beginning to think that is probably the only way to deal with the matter.

maintopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: We wish only to have it workable.	'

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: Without having given the matter particular thought, it strikes me it would be almost impossible, unless we had a constant interchange of what used to be the court, or what is now the appeal board in the district, to provide that there would always be in any district three men who had not as yet dealt with a particular case. maintopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS

maintopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS

maintopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: There is nothing to preclude the chairman of the commission from naming the local board, if he so wishes?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS

maintopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: It seems to me the important point with respect to the section is the dissatisfaction which arises on account of the fact that the appeal court does not actually see the applicant. maintopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: I cannot find any provision in the bill to give the new appeal board power to remit a case to the commission for further consideration, as is provided in section 69 of the act.

maintopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL BOARD AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS

I shall check up on that
point. I imagine there is power, but it does not appear to be stated specifically in the bill.
